name: Zane Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Zane. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, no ties to companies, unions, parties or government, and this is all confidential. Could you tell me what a normal day at work looks like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I push dirt. I'm on a dozer at the Barlow open cut, the coal mine east of town, and mostly I'm cleaning up the benches and pushing the spoil, the waste rock, over the edge after the trucks dump it. Twelve-hour shifts, four on, four off. I like that nobody talks to me for most of it. I don't like the new screen they put in the cab, it beeps at me when I'm off the plan by half a metre.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been on the dozer?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Three years. Before that I was thirty years at the sawmill in Harlan, on the log yard, until the mill shut when the big company bought it and moved everything south. I was fifty-five. Marlene does the books part-time at the hardware store, and between us we pay the bills and not much else. We've got maybe two or three weeks in the bank, no more. I'm still the guy the supervisor sends to the easy jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so. Everyone was going on about it and nothing happened, like the year two thousand thing. I don't go online, so I'd say it at the break table and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Means I keep my job for now. The computer never scared me. What scares me is the boss with a calculator deciding a dozer can drive itself. That's a different thing and that's still there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Turn up, push dirt, try to get better on the steep benches so they stop giving me the easy stuff. Pay the bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the boss with a calculator still worries you. Is there something specific going on at Barlow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They've got a remote dozer on the north side, run by a guy in a room in town. I hear it works about as well as I do, which isn't saying much. Nobody talks about it in front of us, which tells you something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything change at home if things stayed like this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Marlene wants a new fridge, the old one sounds like a tractor. Maybe next year. We're not big spenders, we can't be.

S0.say: He'd say 'I told you so' at the break table, comparing AI to past scares that came to nothing; he doesn't go online.
S0.think: He thinks it means keeping his job for now, but he's still worried about managers deciding a dozer can drive itself, which has nothing to do with clever AI.
S0.do: Keeps turning up and pushing dirt, trying to improve on the steep benches so he stops being given the easy jobs. Keeps paying the bills and maybe replaces the fridge next year.
S0.quote: The computer never scared me. What scares me is the boss with a calculator deciding a dozer can drive itself.
S0.fieldNote: Zane speaks in short, flat sentences and resists drama. Even in the calm picture he points to a remote dozer already working at Barlow, but he files it away as a separate, slower threat. His wishes are small and practical, like replacing a noisy fridge.

steps.text: Keep pushing spoil on the Barlow dozer and get better on the steep benches
Buy Marlene a new fridge next year if the bills allow

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's business, they'll do what makes money. I wouldn't make a big speech. I'd probably say 'let's see what happens' and go back to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, dozers are going to be in the first lot. They've got one on the north side already. I'm the newest and the slowest on the dozers, so if they cut three, I'm one of the three, simple maths.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and hope they need some of us. We'd stop the fridge, stop eating out on Fridays, and Marlene would look for more hours. I wouldn't do any computer course, I'd just make it hard for them to say I'm bad at my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. More than I'd say out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't take a computer course. If the mine offered one with pay, would that change anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe if they paid, I'd sit in the room. But I'd be wasting their time. I can't use the screen in my own cab without swearing at it. My grandson does my phone for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'let's see what happens' in public, but you've just told me you'd be one of the first three. Which is closer to how you really feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The second one. 'Let's see' is just what you say. You don't tell the guys you're scared, they'd never let you forget it. Marlene knows, that's enough.

S1.say: He'd say it's just business, companies will do what makes money, and he'd tell co-workers 'let's see what happens'.
S1.think: He believes dozers will be among the first jobs cut, and as the newest and slowest dozer driver he'd be one of the first to go.
S1.do: Keeps his head down and tries to look indispensable rather than retraining. Cuts the new fridge and Friday meals out while his wife looks for more hours.
S1.feel: Worried, more than he'd admit out loud.
S1.quote: I'm the newest and the slowest on the dozers, so if they cut three, I'm one of the three, simple maths.
S1.fieldNote: There's a clear gap between Zane's public 'let's see' and his private arithmetic that he'd be among the first cut. He won't consider retraining seriously and says so, preferring to make himself hard to fault. He doesn't blame anyone; he calls it business, which fits his middle-of-the-road outlook.

steps.text: Keep his head down and hope the mine keeps some dozer drivers
Drop the new fridge and Friday meals out
Work hard enough on the dozer that nobody can call him bad at it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking work in 2028. That's Marlene's job. The books.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the break table I'd say the robots aren't here till 2031, so we've got a bit yet. I'd say it like I wasn't bothered. Then I'd go and sit in the cab.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's worse than the card makes it sound. That remote dozer on the north side is run by a guy in a room in town, and a computer that can think can sit in that room instead of him, so mine doesn't need any fancy robot. And Marlene's book work at the hardware store goes in 2028 for sure. So we could lose both pays inside a year or two, with three weeks in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the pay office in the first month and ask what my pension looks like if I take it at sixty, even with the chunk they take off. I'd work every overtime shift they'd give me. We'd sell the boat trailer and the second car straight away, maybe 6,000 for both. And I'd ask our daughter if we could lean on her for a while if it came to that, which would kill me to ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the mill all over again, only quicker. I'd be lying awake listening to Marlene breathing and doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Marlene do when the books go to the computer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's sixty, same as me near enough. She'd look for shop floor hours, stocking shelves, that's still hands for a while. But the hardware store's not big, and there's ten people in town who'd want the same hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the card makes it sound better than it is. Why do you think the company would move early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because they already have. Nobody talks about the remote dozer in front of us, and that tells you they're working out the numbers. I've already watched one place shut with me in it, and I didn't think I'd get a second go at that.

S2.say: The robots aren't here till 2031, so we've got a bit yet. I'd say it like I wasn't bothered, then go and sit in the cab.
S2.think: A computer that can think can sit in the remote dozer room in town instead of the operator, so my dozer won't wait for any robot. Marlene's book work at the hardware store goes in 2028 too, so we could lose both pays inside a year or two with three weeks in the bank.
S2.do: Asks the pay office in the first month what his pension would be if taken early at sixty, and works every overtime shift. Sells the boat trailer and second car for about 6,000, and asks their daughter whether they could lean on her if it came to that.
S2.feel: Like the mill closing all over again, only quicker. He'd lie awake doing sums.
S2.quote: I've already watched one place shut with me in it, and I didn't think I'd get a second go at that.
S2.fieldNote: Zane read the card more darkly than it reads, because the remote dozer at his mine means a thinking AI can do his job without waiting for robots. His wife's bookkeeping is exactly the thinking work that goes first, so both incomes are at risk at once. He won't retrain; his plan is an early pension, selling things and leaning on family.

steps.text: Ask the Barlow pay office about taking his pension early at sixty
Sell the boat trailer and the second car for about 6,000
Ask their daughter if they could lean on her for a while

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2031. I'd be sixty-three. That's closer to the pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a long time in mining, half the managers will have changed by then. At the break table I'd say 'let's see', same as always. I'd mean it a bit more this time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the remote dozer room goes to the computer in 2031, and so do Marlene's books. I'd be 63. If I can stretch it to sixty-three with a bit in the bank, I can probably stretch the rest with Marlene finding shop hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save forty or fifty every pay, which means takeaways and the cable TV go straight away. I'd keep turning up and try to be good enough that they keep me to the end. And I'd wait and see if they keep a few dozer drivers on for the jobs the machines can't do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like a long drive with the fuel light on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about learning the remote system in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Five years or two, I'm still the guy who swears at the screen. Some young fella will do the room until the computer takes it. I'd rather keep my seat in the cab as long as they'll let me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's in the bank by 2031 if you save fifty a pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the car doesn’t die, it adds up. Five or six thousand saved is not much, but it’s more than I had when the mill shut, and that counts for something.

S3.say: Five years is a long time in mining, and half the managers will have changed by then. Let's see, same as always.
S3.think: The remote dozer room goes to the computer in 2031, and so do Marlene's books, when I'd be 63. If I can stretch it to sixty-three with a bit in the bank, I can probably stretch the rest with Marlene finding shop hours.
S3.do: Saves forty or fifty every pay by cutting takeaways and cable TV straight away. Keeps turning up and working well enough to be kept to the end, and waits to see if a few dozer drivers are kept for jobs machines can't do.
S3.feel: Anxious, like a long drive with the fuel light on.
S3.quote: Five or six thousand saved is not much, but it’s more than I had when the mill shut, and that counts for something.
S3.fieldNote: With five years Zane can see a path to near his pension, and saving small fixed amounts makes him feel he's doing something. He still refuses to learn the remote system. The memory of the mill closing is his yardstick for everything.

steps.text: Save forty or fifty every pay until 2031
Cancel the takeaways and the cable TV straight away
Wait to see if Barlow keeps a few dozer drivers for the hard jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2036? I'd be sixty-eight. I'd be gone by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's a long way off and I'll be fishing by then. I wouldn't say much else. The guys would joke I'm getting out just in time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years isn't my problem, it's my grandson's problem, and that bothers me more than I thought it would. Kyle's sixteen and wants to drive machines like his grandad. By the time he's any good, the machines will be driving themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, keep putting a little by and pay off the car. I'd tell Kyle not to go into machine driving. That's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not for me. For the boy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Kyle to do instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, and that's the trouble. Something with people, maybe, nursing or the ambulance. I'd tell my grandson Kyle the dozer was good to me for a few years, but it won't be there for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the remote dozer still worry you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, the way it does now. But they've had that thing on the north side for two years and it's still one machine. If the computers don't get clever till 2036, I'll be on my boat by then.

S4.say: That's a long way off and I'll be fishing by then. The guys would joke I'm getting out just in time.
S4.think: Ten years isn't my problem, it's my grandson's problem, and that bothers me more than I thought it would. Kyle wants to drive machines like his grandad, and by the time he's good, they'll drive themselves.
S4.do: Keeps working, keeps putting a little by and pays off the car. Tells his grandson Kyle not to go into machine driving.
S4.feel: Uneasy, but for his grandson rather than himself.
S4.quote: I'd tell my grandson Kyle the dozer was good to me for a few years, but it won't be there for him.
S4.fieldNote: Zane expects to retire well before 2036, so this picture barely touches him. His worry moves to his teenage grandson, who wants to follow him onto machines. He has no clear alternative to offer the boy and admits it.

steps.text: Keep driving the dozer at Barlow until his pension
Put a little by each pay and pay off the car
Tell his grandson Kyle not to go into machine driving

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Marlene's book work goes first and my dozer right after, and you'd have no time and no money and the pension isn't there yet. What would help is being able to take the pension early without losing a big chunk of it, for guys over fifty-five who get pushed out. That, and somebody to do the forms for you.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask why they hire old guys like me if they're only going to get rid of us. I came here because the mill shut. If the mine shuts too, there's nowhere left to come to. That's this town in one sentence.

headlineQuote: I came here because the mill shut. If the mine shuts too, there's nowhere left to come to.
portrait: Zane Schmidt is 58 and drives a dozer at the Barlow open-cut coal mine, a job he took three years ago after thirty years on a sawmill log yard ended when the mill closed. He has two or three weeks of savings, a wife who keeps books part-time, and no taste for screens or computer courses. He calls automation 'business' rather than blaming anyone, says 'let's see' in public, and privately works out that he'd be among the first cut. AGI by 2028 alarms him because his wife's bookkeeping goes first and a thinking computer could run the mine's remote dozer without waiting for robots, so he'd look at an early pension and lean on his daughter. With five years he saves small, fixed amounts, and the ten-year picture worries him mostly for his grandson.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because his wife's bookkeeping and his dozer job could both go within a year or two, with no money saved and no pension yet.
whatWouldHelp: Being able to take his pension early without losing a big part of it if he's pushed out after fifty-five, and someone to help with the forms.
